en: Whilst you can build a single page
application like this by using attributes
like this,
there actually is an easier way of doing
that if your goal is to
give users that single page application like
look and feel.
Instead of setting that target and of using
push URL,
and instead of using hx-get here, you can go
back to our regular anchor element as we had
it before without using HTMX here.
And instead you can add a special attribute
onto the body of your element or on any
parent element of the element that should be
controlled by HTMX. But here I wanna control
all the elements on the page with HTMX
because the attribute I'll add here on this
body element is hx-boost.
And that should be set to true here.
Now, what does hx-boost do though?
Well,
this attribute boosts all
anchor elements to be controlled by HTMX.
And what that means is that now with
hx-boost added here,
all
those anchor elements will actually send a
GET request to their target URL
and will swap the body of the current page
for the body of the incoming response.
So essentially, we'll get the behavior we
had before
but without manually adding hx-get and
hx-target here and so on.
We also don't need to manually update the
URL because that will also be done by
hx-boost.
So in the end, hx-boost is there to simplify
the process of building such a single page
application.
Because with it added here to this body on
this page that renders all products,
if I save that and reload, you see I get the
same behavior as before.
The URL is updated and I can use the back
button
and this refresh icon never changes to a
cross.
I got that same behavior, but now
this works with help of hx-boost. And
therefore, if you wanna build such a single
page application
where you technically never leave the
current page, you can easily do that with
hx-boost, which will convert all anchor
elements to HTMX-controlled anchor elements.
And it'll do even more than that.
